It explores possibilities using recursion and prunes branches early to reduce the search space. Common uses include solving puzzles like Sudoku, generating permutations, and the N-Queens problem.

nodes.name: Brute Force
nodes.description: Brute force solves a problem by trying every possible solution and returning the one that works. It requires no insight into the problem structure and always finds a correct answer if one exists. The trade-off is poor efficiency: brute force is often exponential or factorial in time and only practical for small inputs.

resources.title: Brute Force Algorithm Explained With C++ Examples

nodes.name: Greedy Algorithms
nodes.description: Greedy algorithms make the locally optimal choice at each step with the hope that this leads to a globally optimal solution. They are fast and simple but do not always produce the best result. Problems where greedy works correctly include activity selection, Huffman encoding, and finding minimum spanning trees.

nodes.name: Randomised Algorithms
nodes.description: Randomized algorithms use random numbers as part of their logic, either to avoid worst-case behavior or to approximate solutions. Quicksort with a random pivot is a classic example: randomization makes the worst case very unlikely in practice. Monte Carlo and Las Vegas algorithms are the two main categories.

nodes.name: Island traversal
nodes.description: Island traversal refers to problems where a 2D grid is searched to identify and count connected regions, often called islands, surrounded by water or empty space. It is typically solved using DFS or BFS starting from unvisited land cells, marking each reachable cell as visited. This pattern generalizes to many connected-component problems.

nodes.name: Divide and Conquer
nodes.description: Divide and conquer is a powerful algorithm design technique that solves a problem by breaking it down into smaller and easier-to-manage sub-problems, until these become simple enough to be solved directly. This approach is usually carried out recursively for most problems. Once all the sub-problems are solved, the solutions are combined to give a solution to the original problem. It is a common strategy that significantly reduces the complexity of the problem.

resources.title: Merge Sort in Python: Step-by-Step Guide + Code

nodes.name: Multi-threaded
nodes.description: Multi-threaded algorithms divide work across multiple threads running concurrently, using parallelism to reduce total execution time. Designing them correctly requires managing shared state to avoid race conditions and deadlocks. Parallel merge sort and parallel BFS are examples where multi-threading provides meaningful speedups.

resources.title: Python Multithreading: The Most Practical Intro

nodes.name: Leetcode
nodes.description: LeetCode is the most widely used platform for technical interview preparation. It offers thousands of problems categorized by topic and difficulty, with a built-in code editor and test runner. Many interview candidates use LeetCode's problem sets specifically because they reflect the style and content of questions asked at major tech companies.

nodes.name: Recursion
nodes.description: Recursion is a technique where a function calls itself with a smaller version of the problem until reaching a base case. It maps naturally to problems with recursive structure, such as tree traversal, divide and conquer, and backtracking. Understanding the call stack and how recursive calls unwind is key to using recursion correctly.

resources.title: Merge Sort in Python: Step-by-Step Guide + Code

nodes.name: Kth Element
nodes.description: The Kth element problem asks for the k-th smallest or largest element in an unsorted array without fully sorting it. Efficient solutions include using a min-heap or max-heap of size k, or the quickselect algorithm, which runs in O(n) average time. This problem pattern appears frequently in data stream processing.

nodes.name: Two Heaps
nodes.description: The two heaps technique uses a max-heap and a min-heap together to efficiently track the median or partition a dataset. One heap holds the lower half of elements and the other holds the upper half, keeping them balanced so the median is always accessible in O(1). It is used in problems that require continuous median tracking over a data stream.

resources.title: Two Heaps — A Coding Pattern for Median-finding (Emre Bolat)

nodes.name: Edabit
nodes.description: Edabit is a coding practice platform that focuses on smaller, beginner-friendly challenges designed to build programming fluency quickly. Problems are shorter and more approachable than those on LeetCode, making it a good starting point for learners who are still developing confidence with code before moving to interview-style questions.

nodes.name: Dynamic Programming
nodes.description: Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems and storing the results to avoid redundant computation. It applies when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems. Classic examples include the Fibonacci sequence, knapsack problem, and longest common subsequence.

resources.title: Getting Started with Dynamic Programming in Data Structures and Algorithms
What Is Dynamic Programming and How To Use It
5 Simple Steps for Solving Dynamic Programming Problems

nodes.name: Merge Intervals
nodes.description: Merge intervals is a technique for solving problems involving overlapping ranges. The typical approach sorts intervals by start time, then iterates through them, merging any that overlap with the previous one. It is used in calendar scheduling, resource allocation, and range consolidation problems.

nodes.name: Two Pointer Technique
nodes.description: The two pointer technique uses two indices that move through an array or list to solve problems more efficiently than nested loops. One common pattern starts both pointers at opposite ends and moves them inward. It is used to find pairs with a target sum, remove duplicates, and solve partitioning problems in O(n) time.

resources.title: Mastering the Two Pointers Technique: An In-Depth Guide

nodes.name: Cyclic Sort
nodes.description: Cyclic sort is a sorting technique for arrays whose values fall in a known, contiguous range, typically `1` to `n`. Each element is swapped to the position matching its value, placing everything correctly in O(n) time and O(1) space — ideal as a building block for problems such as finding missing or duplicate numbers.

nodes.name: Sliding Window Technique
nodes.description: The sliding window technique maintains a subset of elements within a fixed or variable-size window that moves across a sequence. As the window slides, elements are added at one end and removed from the other, avoiding the need to recompute results from scratch. It is used to find maximum subarrays, longest substrings, and other contiguous subset problems in O(n) time.

nodes.name: Fast and Slow Pointers
nodes.description: The fast and slow pointers pattern uses two pointers that traverse a data structure at different speeds. It is commonly used to detect cycles in linked lists, find the middle of a list, or locate the kth element from the end, running in O(n) time with constant space.

nodes.name: Platforms to Practice
nodes.description: Practice platforms provide coding problems, judge submissions automatically, and track progress over time. Regular practice on these platforms builds problem-solving speed and familiarity with common patterns. Consistent repetition across a variety of problem types is the most reliable way to prepare for technical interviews.
